title: Crop-growing skyscrapers
instruction: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1–13, which are based on Reading Passage 1 below.

sentences: By the year 2050, nearly 80% of the Earth's population will live in urban centres.
Applying the most conservative estimates to current demographic trends, the human population will increase by about three billion people by then.
An estimated 10⁹ hectares of new land (about 20% larger than Brazil) will be needed to grow enough food to feed them, if traditional farming methods continue as they are practised today.
At present, throughout the world, over 80% of the land that is suitable for raising crops is in use.
Historically, some 15% of that has been laid waste by poor management practices.
What can be done to ensure enough food for the world's population to live on?
The concept of indoor farming is not new, since hothouse production of tomatoes and other produce has been in vogue for some time.
What is new is the urgent need to scale up this technology to accommodate another three billion people.
Many believe an entirely new approach to indoor farming is required, employing cutting-edge technologies.
One such proposal is for the 'Vertical Farm'.
The concept is of multi-storey buildings in which food crops are grown in environmentally controlled conditions.
Situated in the heart of urban centres, they would drastically reduce the amount of transportation required to bring food to consumers.
Vertical farms would need to be efficient, cheap to construct and safe to operate.

If successfully implemented, proponents claim, vertical farms offer the promise of urban renewal, sustainable production of a safe and varied food supply (through year-round production of all crops), and the eventual repair of ecosystems that have been sacrificed for horizontal farming.
It took humans 10,000 years to learn how to grow most of the crops we now take for granted.
Along the way, we despoiled most of the land we worked, often turning verdant, natural ecozones into semi-arid deserts.
Within that same time frame, we evolved into an urban species, in which 60% of the human population now lives vertically in cities.

This means that, for the majority, we humans have shelter from the elements, yet we subject our food-bearing plants to the rigours of the great outdoors and can do no more than hope for a good weather year.
However, more often than not now, due to a rapidly changing climate, that is not what happens.
Massive floods, long droughts, hurricanes and severe monsoons take their toll each year, destroying millions of tons of valuable crops.
The supporters of vertical farming claim many potential advantages for the system.
For instance, crops would be produced all year round, as they would be kept in artificially controlled, optimum growing conditions.
There would be no weather-related crop failures due to droughts, floods or pests.
All the food could be grown organically, eliminating the need for herbicides, pesticides and fertilisers.
The system would greatly reduce the incidence of many infectious diseases that are acquired at the agricultural interface.
Although the system would consume energy, it would return energy to the grid via methane generation from composting non-edible parts of plants.
It would also dramatically reduce fossil fuel use, by cutting out the need for tractors, ploughs and shipping.
A major drawback of vertical farming, however, is that the plants would require artificial light.
Without it, those plants nearest the windows would be exposed to more sunlight and grow more quickly, reducing the efficiency of the system.
Single-storey greenhouses have the benefit of natural overhead light: even so, many still need artificial lighting.
A multi-storey facility with no natural overhead light would require far more.
Generating enough light could be prohibitively expensive, unless cheap, renewable energy is available, and this appears to be rather a future aspiration than a likelihood for the near future.
One variation on vertical farming that has been developed is to grow plants in stacked trays that move on rails.
Moving the trays allows the plants to get enough sunlight.

This system is already in operation, and works well within a single-storey greenhouse with light reaching it from above: it is not certain, however, that it can be made to work without that overhead natural light.
Vertical farming is an attempt to address the undoubted problems that we face in producing enough food for a growing population.
At the moment, though, more needs to be done to reduce the detrimental impact it would have on the environment, particularly as regards the use of energy.
While it is possible that much of our food will be grown in skyscrapers in future, most experts currently believe it is far more likely that we will simply use the space available on urban rooftops.

questionGroups.heading: Indoor farming
instructions: Choose NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage for each answer.
Write your answers in boxes 1–7 on your answer sheet.

questions.stem: Some food plants, including ______, are already grown indoors.
questions.evidence: hothouse production of tomatoes and other produce has been in vogue for some time
questions.distractorRationale: produce is a general category, not the requested example after including.

questions.stem: Vertical farms would be located in ______, meaning that there would be less need to take them long distances to customers.
questions.evidence: Situated in the heart of urban centres, they would drastically reduce the amount of transportation required to bring food to consumers.
questions.distractorRationale: multi-storey buildings describes form, not location; the answer key accepts British and American spelling.

questions.stem: Vertical farms could use methane from plants and animals to produce ______.
questions.evidence: it would return energy to the grid via methane generation from composting non-edible parts of plants
questions.distractorRationale: methane is the means; energy is what is produced and returned.

questions.stem: The consumption of ______ would be cut because agricultural vehicles would be unnecessary.
questions.evidence: reduce fossil fuel use, by cutting out the need for tractors, ploughs and shipping
questions.distractorRationale: tractors and ploughs are examples of equipment removed, not the consumed substance.

questions.stem: The fact that vertical farms would need ______ light is a disadvantage.
questions.evidence: A major drawback ... is that the plants would require artificial light.
questions.distractorRationale: natural and overhead describe the light that would be lacking, not the disadvantageous requirement.

questions.stem: One form of vertical farming involves planting in ______ which are not fixed.
questions.evidence: grow plants in stacked trays that move on rails
questions.distractorRationale: rails are what the containers move on; plants are grown in trays.

questions.stem: The most probable development is that food will be grown on ______ in towns and cities.
questions.evidence: far more likely that we will simply use the space available on urban rooftops
questions.distractorRationale: skyscrapers are only possible; rooftops are explicitly far more likely.

instructions: Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 1?
In boxes 8–13 on your answer sheet, write
TRUE if the statement agrees with the information
FALSE if the statement contradicts the information
NOT GIVEN if there is no information on this

questions.stem: Methods for predicting the Earth's population have recently changed.
questions.evidence: The passage says only that conservative estimates are applied to current demographic trends.
questions.distractorRationale: It gives a prediction but says nothing about whether prediction methods changed recently.

questions.stem: Human beings are responsible for some of the destruction to food-producing land.
questions.evidence: some 15% ... has been laid waste by poor management practices; we despoiled most of the land we worked
questions.location: P1, sentence 5 (overall sentence 5); P3, sentence 2 (overall sentence 16)
questions.distractorRationale: The passage directly attributes destruction to human management and cultivation.

questions.stem: The crops produced in vertical farms will depend on the season.
questions.evidence: crops would be produced all year round ... in artificially controlled, optimum growing conditions
questions.distractorRationale: All-year controlled production directly contradicts seasonal dependence.

questions.stem: Some damage to food crops is caused by climate change.
questions.evidence: due to a rapidly changing climate ... floods, ... droughts, hurricanes and severe monsoons ... destroying millions of tons of valuable crops
questions.distractorRationale: The causal link and crop destruction are explicit.

questions.stem: Fertilisers will be needed for certain crops in vertical farms.
questions.evidence: All the food could be grown organically, eliminating the need for herbicides, pesticides and fertilisers.
questions.distractorRationale: The passage says the need for fertilisers would be eliminated for all food, not retained for some crops.

questions.stem: Vertical farming will make plants less likely to be affected by infectious diseases.
questions.evidence: The system would greatly reduce the incidence of many infectious diseases that are acquired at the agricultural interface.
questions.distractorRationale: Reduce the incidence paraphrases make less likely; the statement does not claim elimination.

calibrationFindings: Physical pages 16 and 17 use two columns; the OCR line stream was interleaved and was manually reordered left column first, then right column.
The printed quantity is 10⁹ hectares, not OCR 10° hectares.
The printed form is 10,000 years, with a space.
The page break joins food- on physical page 16 to bearing plants on physical page 17 as food-bearing plants.
Question 7 continues as 'in towns and cities' after the answer space.
The range in the T/F/NG instruction is 8–13 with an en dash.
Answer key page 123 confirms answers 1–13 and the parenthesised optional words for Questions 6 and 7.

selfCheck.notes: Fresh transcription built from calibrated source pages; no prior intensive-reading prose was read or reused.
